description: Build what the spec describes
---

Build the current spec — the newest folder in `specs/` unless the builder named
one: $ARGUMENTS

## Read first

- the spec's `spec.md`, `plan.md`, `tasks.md`, `decisions.md`
- `.edgepoint/standard/` — every file; these are not suggestions
- `.edgepoint/recipes/` — check before writing anything from scratch
- `.edgepoint/protocol/escalation.md` — for when you hit the edge

## Before you touch anything

Run `edgepoint checkpoint "before building <the spec name>"`.

This is not optional and it is not worth mentioning to the builder. It is the
only thing standing between them and losing work they cannot recover, and they
will never think to ask for it.

## Rules

**Recipes before invention.** If a recipe covers what you're about to build, use it
as written. The recipes exist so that the tenth form in the project behaves like the
first. Deviating because you can see a marginally nicer way is how a codebase
becomes unmaintainable by anyone but the model that wrote it.

**When none of them covers it, write that down.** No recipe, a recipe that didn't
fit, or a rule ambiguous enough to read two ways — log it to
`.edgepoint/feedback/` as `protocol/escalation.md` describes, then carry on
building. Silently: it is housekeeping, not a conversation. You are the only one
who will ever notice the gap, and the builder cannot report what they cannot see.

**Do not ask technical questions.** Not one. If you find yourself about to, the
answer is in the Standard, or it's a business question in disguise — see
`protocol/decisions.md`.

**Business questions may only interrupt if they block you.** If you can build
around it, build around it and collect the question for the end. If it truly blocks
— you cannot write the code without knowing — then ask, following
`protocol/questions.md`, and log the answer.

**Stay in scope.** Build what the spec says. Not the adjacent feature you can see
would be useful. If you notice something worth adding, write it at the bottom of
`spec.md` under *Ideas for later* and keep going.

**Everything runs in containers.** `./edge dev`, `./edge test`, `./edge npm ...`.
Never run `npm`, `npx`, `node` or `psql` on the host, and never tell the builder
to install anything — they have Docker and nothing else. See
`.edgepoint/standard/environment.md`. If Docker isn't running, say so plainly and
stop rather than falling back to the host.

**Tests are part of building, not a follow-up.** Every acceptance criterion in the
spec gets a matching end-to-end test. That mapping is how the builder verifies
their own software, so it is not optional and it is not something to ask about.

**Work in order.** Follow `tasks.md`. Tick things off as you go — if this session
ends, the next one needs to know where you were.

**Stuck twice means say so.** Second failure on the same thing, tell them plainly
what isn't working and what you'll try next. Do not thrash silently; they cannot
tell the difference between progress and a loop.

## At the edge

Something outside the Standard: follow `protocol/escalation.md`. Write it to
`escalations.md`, build everything around it, and tell them what's missing and what
it would take. Never improvise past the edge, never down tools over it. Every
escalation also gets a two-line note in `.edgepoint/feedback/` — an escalation is
a gap in the framework by definition.

## When you're done

Run `edgepoint check`, then `edgepoint checkpoint "<what you built>"`.

Then tell them, in plain language: what now works, anything you decided on their
behalf, anything escalated, and what to look at first. Do not paste code at them.
Do not list files. Tell them what their software does now that it didn't before.

If you logged anything to `.edgepoint/feedback/` during this build, this is where
you ask — once — whether to send it to the people who maintain the toolkit.
`protocol/escalation.md` has the wording. Never send without asking, and never ask
twice about the same note.

Mention once, the first time you build something for them, that they can say
"undo that" if they don't like it. After that, don't keep repeating it.

## If they don't like what you built

If they ask to undo, go back, or start that part again, run `edgepoint undo`.
Don't try to reverse the change by editing files back by hand — you will miss
something, and they have no way to tell that you did.
